items.title: What holds and what breaks: Boundary objects in AI-enabled curriculum governance
items.abstract: Universities govern AI adoption through artefacts. Policies, rubrics, assessment briefs, vendor evaluation frameworks, and design templates cross organisational boundaries and carry meaning differently in each context. This paper applies the concept of boundary objects within a cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse which artefacts effectively mediate AI governance across academic, institutional, and commercial activity systems, and which fail. Drawing on the author’s framework for negotiated legitimacy in interacting activity systems and reflexive practitioner experience as an education design leader, the paper develops a typology of AI governance boundary objects classified by origin, interpretive flexibility, and failure mode. The analysis identifies three structural conditions that determine whether a boundary object supports or undermines the legitimacy of learning designers who broker AI adoption across systems. These are co-design across activity systems, support for transformation rather than coordination alone, and resistance to capture by a single system’s logic. It also identifies a failure dynamic specific to generative AI, in which an unstable referent causes artefacts to decay. The paper offers practical design principles for governance artefacts and connects them to a wider question, namely how institutions keep human and pedagogical judgement central as they adopt digital technologies.

items.title: What makes AI educational? A sociocultural framework for transforming AI from artefact to mediating tool
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.

items.title: When AI Becomes a “Colleague”: How Anthropomorphism and Cognitive Support Shape the Demand-Cyberloafing Link in Human–AI Collaboration
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in the workplace, limited research has examined how job demands shape employees’ behavioral and motivational responses in human–AI collaboration and how resources influence these relationships. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, this study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining semi-structured interviews with 15 participants (10 employees and 5 graduate students) to explore relevant job demands and resources, followed by a cross-sectional survey yielding 282 valid responses to test the research model. The findings show that job demand is positively associated with cyberloafing and negatively associated with job engagement. Anthropomorphism strengthens the positive association between job demand and cyberloafing while weakening its negative association with job engagement. Cognitive support also strengthens the former relationship but does not significantly moderate the latter. These findings extend JD-R theory to human–AI collaboration by highlighting the differentiated roles of resources across behavioral and motivational outcomes. They also suggest that anthropomorphic AI may help sustain job engagement under demanding conditions, while its association with cyberloafing warrants careful consideration.

items.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

items.title: When AI talks back: A cross-disciplinary study of educator design judgment in AI-assisted case development
items.abstract: Educators are increasingly turning to generative AI when developing teaching materials, yet most research to date has centred on student-facing applications. This paper presents a work-in-progress study that asks a different question: what happens to an educator’s design judgment when AI enters the case-writing process? Two business educators – one in accounting, one in management – will each develop a teaching case study using AI-assisted workflows, documenting their prompts, editorial decisions, and reasoning through structured process logs. Drawing on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner framework and Abell’s (1997) 10 criteria for effective teaching cases, the study examines where human expertise proves essential and where AI contributes meaningfully. The pairing of two sub-disciplines, management accounting and management, allows us to examine whether disciplinary knowledge shapes these design decisions in distinct ways, although the study’s central concern remain the design judgement itself. Early observations from the instrument development phase point to a useful distinction: AI appears better suited to qualities that require evaluative judgment (structure, data accuracy, length) than those demanding generative judgment (ambiguity, controversy, authentic voice). We expect further patterns to emerge once data collection begins. This paper outlines the research design and its anticipated contributions.

items.title: When connection requires refusal: AI backlash and accountable technology design in higher education
items.abstract: This non-empirical conceptual analysis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming woven into curriculum production, assessment, feedback, student support, academic integrity, accessibility and institutional decision-making. These systems are often justified through connection: faster feedback, personalised support, scalable services and more efficient learning design. Yet technical connection is not the same as educational connection. AI may leave the visible forms of university learning intact while weakening academic authorship, assessment validity, student trust, staff agency, care, equity and institutional legitimacy. The paper develops refusal-capable design: the distributed institutional capacity to decide when AI should be adopted, constrained, redesigned or refused. It integrates connected learning, responsible innovation, sociotechnical studies of educational technology, care ethics, justice-oriented educational judgment and technology non-use scholarship, using selected public examples illustratively rather than as an empirical sample. Six heuristic refusal zones organise recurring legitimacy tensions, and the Distributed Refusal-Capable University Design Cycle translates those tensions into accountable redesign. The contribution is a practical and theoretical account of refusal as a legitimate design outcome rather than simple opposition to AI.

items.title: When GenAI enters the assessment relationship: Public expectations of transparency, judgement and responsibility
items.abstract: Human-centred learning design requires more than using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to make assessment feedback faster, more accessible or scalable. It requires attention to whether human judgement, relationships and responsibility remain visible when feedback is produced. The public is a key stakeholder in these decisions because university qualifications operate as public credentials whose legitimacy depends on confidence in how achievement is judged and certified. Yet debate has largely focused on students’ use of GenAI, with less attention given to public expectations of academic practice when GenAI contributes to feedback. This exploratory study surveyed 299 participants, most of whom had current or previous experience of higher education, to examine the implied obligations underpinning university assessment and feedback. Participants strongly endorsed feedback as an expected component of university teaching and generally supported disclosure of GenAI use, meaningful academic involvement and visible instructor responsibility. Exploratory factor analysis identified two provisional dimensions: AI feedback transparency and legitimacy, and assessment expectations and feedback value, although the second demonstrated only modest internal consistency. Interpreted through psychological contract theory, the findings suggest that human-centred GenAI implementation depends not only on feedback quality or efficiency but also on preserving visible academic judgement, accountability and educational purpose. The central design distinction is therefore between GenAI that supports academic practice and GenAI that substitutes for meaningful academic engagement.

items.title: When social interaction becomes an algorithm: AI-mediated education, intercultural competence, and the risks to democratic schooling
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational settings has been increasingly framed as a transformative opportunity for learning, especially in relation to Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) and Intercultural Competence (IC). Generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms, including conversational interfaces and adaptive feedback mechanisms, are increasingly positioned as tools for mediating educational interactions (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes & Tuomi, 2022). However, this assumption obscures a critical issue. Research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) highlights that educational AI encompasses diverse technological applications and involves not only technological design but also questions concerning adoption, impacts, challenges, and the ways in which such systems shape teaching and learning processes (Wang et al., 2024). From a critical perspective, generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms can therefore be understood not as neutral tools, but as sociotechnical infrastructures that may reflect and reproduce certain epistemological, cultural, and political assumptions about what counts as information, knowledge, communication, appropriate social interaction, and educational practice (Williamson & Eynon, 2020).In this sense, AI-mediated education refers not simply to the use of educational systems, particularly generative and adaptive learning systems, in classrooms, but to the reconfiguration of educational relationships through algorithmic systems that intervene between teachers, learners, knowledge, and peers (Kuhail et al., 2023). The convergence of generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms may increasingly shape educational processes through prediction, optimisation, and algorithmic mediation (Turvey & Pachler, 2026;Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). Instead of direct human-to-human interaction, educational processes increasingly take the form of mediated exchanges, such as student-AI-teacher or student-AI-student interactions, enabled particularly by generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems, where algorithms may shape, filter, or mediate elements of dialogue, collaboration, feedback, and critical thinking (Bayne, 2024;Williamson et al., 2020).It is important to note that AI-mediated education does not refer to a homogeneous category of technologies. Contemporary educational AI includes generative AI systems (i.e., large language model-based tutors and conversational agents), adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment tools, machine translation technologies, and other data-driven educational systems that operate through different technical architectures and pedagogical logics (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Recent scholarship has highlighted substantial variation in the degree of human control, automation, stakeholder involvement, and educational mediation across systems (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). The present opinion paper focuses primarily on generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, because these technologies can increasingly mediate educational interactions, shape learning pathways, and influence how learners may encounter knowledge, feedback, and social relations. Consequently, the arguments outlined here should not be interpreted as applying equally to all forms of educational AI. While some applications, such as machine translation and accessibility tools, may facilitate communication and participation without fundamentally restructuring educational relationships, generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may raise more substantial questions regarding algorithmic mediation, epistemic authority, and the democratic purposes of education. Accordingly, the potential consequences discussed in the following sections are considered primarily in relation to generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, rather than being generalised across all educational AI technologies.This transformation is particularly significant for domains such as SEL and IC, both of which depend on exposure to difference, relational engagement, and negotiation of meaning (Deardorff, 2006;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). SEL in this opinion paper is understood in its main formulation as a framework for developing various competencies, such as self-awareness and social awareness, self-management, and relationship skills (CASEL, 2021). However, SEL is not just a set of individual competencies, but a socially, culturally, and relationally embedded process, through which learners understand emotions, norms, and relationships, negotiate social meanings, encounter different perspectives, and develop the capacity to engage constructively with disagreement. From this perspective, SEL depends not only on emotional regulation but also on participation in shared spaces of dialogue and collective meaning. SEL is consequently a situated process that intersects with power, identity and communication within educational contexts.The connection between SEL and IC can be understood more explicitly through their shared relational and dialogical foundations. In Deardorff's (2006) conceptualisation, intercultural competence is not limited to the acquisition of knowledge about cultural groups but involves attitudes, skills, and dispositions that are developed through engagement with cultural difference, including openness, respect, perspective-taking, and the ability to negotiate meaning. Similarly, contemporary approaches to SEL emphasise that social-emotional capacities develop through relationships, communication, perspective-taking, and the interpretation of social situations rather than through isolated individual skill acquisition (CASEL, 2021;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). From a relational and dialogical perspective, these processes necessarily involve encounters with perspectives that are not fully predictable or identical to one's own. Ambiguity and disagreement therefore constitute not merely potential difficulties but important conditions for developing interpretive flexibility, perspective-taking, and the capacity to negotiate meaning. Democratic educational theory further extends this relational logic by positioning plurality, dialogue, and constructive disagreement as conditions of participation in a shared world (Biesta, 2022;Dewey, 1916Dewey, /2018;;Freire, 1970Freire, /2005)). Taken together, these perspectives suggest that SEL and IC share a common relational foundation: both are developed through encounters with others, negotiation of meaning, engagement with difference, and the capacity to remain open to perspectives that cannot be fully predetermined. Democratic schooling provides the broader collective context in which these capacities can be enacted, tested, and developed through participation and dialogue.From this perspective, SEL is sustained not only through emotional regulation but through ambiguity, co-construction, dialogue, and the negotiation of disagreement⎯conditions that may sit uneasily with high predictive and optimisation-oriented forms of algorithmic mediation (Mesquita et al., 2026). Empirical research on generative AI and AI-supported translation tools suggests that these technologies may support intercultural learning by facilitating communication, translation, and access to multiple perspectives (Akhrenova & Moradkhani, 2026). However, this form of mediation also raises theoretical and normative concerns about standardisation, cultural bias, and the possibility that AI may mediate rather than simply facilitate intercultural encounters (Ali et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Consequently, it also raises critical questions about the nature of social interaction, the role of disagreement, and the conditions under which intercultural and democratic learning take place (Andreotti, 2021;CoE, 2018).Therefore, this opinion paper aims to critically examine how AI-mediated educational settings reconfigure social interaction and to explore the conditions under which such mediation may either strengthen or constrain IC, SEL, and democratic schooling. Rather than treating generative AI and adaptive learning systems as inherently harmful or beneficial, the paper focuses on the pedagogical and relational conditions under which AI-mediated interaction may expand participation, access, and opportunities for dialogue, while also potentially reshaping the conditions of interpersonal and democratic engagement.Towards this endeavour, we first argue that AI-mediated education is not a neutral enhancement of learning, but a form of algorithmic mediation that may shape how learners encounter knowledge, others, and difference (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Second, we argue that although AI may enhance accessibility and communication, it may also potentially reduce some forms of ambiguity, unpredictability, and productive tension that are theoretically important to both intercultural and social-emotional learning (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Third, we argue that generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may contribute to the individualisation of learning and the optimisation of interaction, potentially constraining collective meaning-making processes that are essential to democratic education (Biesta, 2022;Selwyn, 2019). Finally, we argue that generative AI and adaptive learning systems should be understood as supplementary technologies within democratically governed educational frameworks rather than as substitutes for human relationality and dialogical engagement (Wieczorek, 2025;Jin & Wang, 2025). This aligns with calls for democratically governed approaches to educational AI that foreground collective oversight, ethical accountability, and participatory design in the development and deployment of AI systems in education (Kerssens & van Es, 2025).The theoretical contribution of this opinion paper lies not in introducing algorithmic sociality as a new concept, but in extending its analytical relevance to educational interaction. We argue that algorithmic sociality helps explain a dimension that is less directly captured by accounts of algorithmic governance, datafication, platformisation, or technological mediation: how changes in the mode of mediation can reconfigure the relational conditions of educational encounter. items.title: Who gets heard in digital learning environments? Rebalancing knowledge sharing across generations and cultures
items.abstract: This conceptual position paper reframes knowledge sharing as informal peer learning in digitally mediated professional environments. It addresses a gap in existing knowledge-sharing and socio-technical explanations which do not sufficiently explain how social conditions interact with digital mechanisms to shape both contribution and recognition. Using theory adaptation and model development, the paper integrates cultural context, generational identity, relational conditions, self-determined motivation, and a cross-cutting socio-digital mediation environment. The model distinguishes willingness to share, opportunity to participate, and the subsequent visibility and recognition of contributions. Its propositions explain how psychological safety mediates contextual influences, how opportunity, power, and risk condition motivation, and how platform affordances and algorithmic visibility shape participation and recognition. The contribution is a human-centred framework for analysing who contributes, who remains silent, and whose knowledge becomes visible and valued, while informing more inclusive workplace learning, professional learning networks, and digitally mediated communities of practice.

items.title: Whose appraisal? A Freire-informed, think-aloud study of allied health students’ use of Generative AI in evidence appraisal
items.abstract: Background Generative AI (GenAI) can now produce artefacts such as essays, literature reviews, and worked rationales which challenge assessment designs that reward the products of thinking over the practice of it (Bearman et al., 2024; Corbin et al., 2025; Dawson et al., 2024). In evidence-based practice (EBP) education, students are required to appraise study quality, interpret effect sizes, and integrate findings into clinical decisions (Lehane et al., 2019). GenAI can now generate convincing outputs for each of these tasks. Observational data on what students do cognitively when they use GenAI in EBP tasks are scarce. Depending on how students use it, GenAI may scaffold the reasoning that EBP education is designed to develop or may bypass it (Vendrell & Johnston, 2026). Aim This study explores how allied health students engage with GenAI, how much they rely on it, and how they reason about its use when completing an EBP evidence-appraisal task. Methods This is an exploratory qualitative study using a concurrent think-aloud protocol with allied health students who have completed an EBP unit. The unit must have included critical reasoning as a learning outcome. Participants complete a structured 60-minute EBP task involving a clinical scenario. During this task, participants verbalise their reasoning and rationale for using or declining GenAI. A researcher facilitates this process through non-directive questions. Sessions are audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed in two stages. In the first stage, transcripts are coded deductively and inductively against the six critical thinking processes in Vendrell and Johnston’s (2026) framework: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity. This stage identifies whether and how reasoning is handed over to GenAI. In the second stage, an interpretive analysis informed by critical pedagogy (Freire, 2005) examines how students position themselves in relation to AI-generated knowledge. Freire described a banking model of education, in which an authority deposits knowledge into passive students. This model offers a lens for examining uncritical acceptance of GenAI output, should that be present (Freire, 2005). Freire located authority in the school system and in the teacher who deposits knowledge into students (Freire, 2005). GenAI is a further candidate for that position in higher education. Unlike a teacher or an institution, it is designed by companies whose incentive is engagement and commercial return rather than student learning (Bartsch et al., 2025). Findings Data collection is in progress. This study will generate think-aloud data on how allied health students engage cognitively with GenAI during EBP appraisal tasks, mapping where GenAI use aligns with or diverges from the reasoning processes EBP education is designed to develop. The interpretive analysis will explore the degrees of agency students exercise over AI-generated knowledge and the conditions in which they exercise or relinquish it, which process-level coding alone cannot capture. Conclusion Findings may inform teaching and assessment design in EBP units and provide a think-aloud protocol that can be adapted to examine GenAI use in reasoning tasks across health professions education.

items.title: Workplace learning and AI challenges: causes and effects
items.abstract: Purpose The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in workplaces is rapidly increasing in our society. This means that AI is fundamentally reshaping workplaces, how tasks are performed and how the authors interact with colleagues. This study aims to develop explanatory knowledge about the challenges of AI-augmented workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative and deductive research approach was applied. Key challenges discovered in the literature review were used as predefined themes to identify and analyse empirical data. Findings The authors have identified five key challenges: AI Strategy, AI Education, Control, Meaningfulness and Integrated Work Processes for Human-AI Collaboration. These challenges were examined in terms of their causes and effects, and an explanatory model (AICH) was developed. Research limitations/implications The study collected data from five companies, which provides some generality beyond this study’s empirical domain. However, it poses challenges in making broader generalisations. Future research could be designed as broader studies to confirm, modify or challenge the findings. Practical implications The findings contribute to workplace learning and provide a basis for identifying risks and potential measures. Social implications The identified challenges regarding AI-assisted workplaces will most likely have broader social ramifications, affecting employees’ overall well-being and company culture. Originality/value The authors do not claim that the challenges per se are new. However, the authors claim that the models consisting of explanatory knowledge visualised as cause-and-effect models are new.

items.abstract: This study investigates the reliability trap in Google Lens, an artificial intelligence-driven augmented reality translation tool. Viewing translation as human-computer interaction, this qualitative field study evaluates artificial intelligence algorithms in the Polish-to-English direction, for so-called incidental texts (text encountered in public spaces, such as signs, notices, and instructions). Analysis indicates that while neural networks deliver high grammatical fluency, their spatial context-blindness to physical geosemiotics causes severe pragmatic pitfalls affecting users, including safety, as well as legal and socio-economic risks. To address this, the paper advocates that traditional equivalence-based quality assessment must give way to a risk management paradigm. Ultimately, operating safely within the augmented linguistic landscape would entail fostering machine translation literacy and risk-aware artificial intelligence interface design.

items.title: "Can a Robot Really Care About Me?" How Perceiving a Tutor as Human or AI Affects Computer Science Students' Attitudes and Experiences
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

items.title: “Feels like a small God”: A multicountry thematic analysis of imaginations of generative AI among users seeking emotional and mental health support.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for emotional and mental health support (EMS), a process in which users often described GenAI as empathic and friend-like. These descriptions suggest that people may develop imaginations of GenAI chatbots that may reflect their interpersonal needs and desires. The objective of this study is to systematically explore and thematically organizethe imaginations of GenAI among users who repeatedly use GenAI for EMS. In April 2024, we recruited 270 adults from 29 countries who had repeatedly utilized GenAI for EMS. Participants provided qualitative data regarding their imagination of ChatGPT. The analysis followed a structured reflexive thematic analysis approach. We identified two meta- themes: a) Entity (the “what”), which described the kind of beings or things they imagine GenAI as, appearing in 86.3% ( n = 233) of responses, and b) Trait (the "how"), which described users’ descriptions of perceived capacities of these beings, appearing in 36% (n = 96) of responses. The “Entity” descriptions clustered along two dimensions : abstract–concrete and human–nonhuman, which intersect to form a four-quadrant conceptual space containing 11 subthemes ranging from unbounded energy and spiritual beings to humans and robots . The “Traits” meta-theme fell into five themes: physical traits and manifestations (“looking”), cognitive abilities (“knowing”), productivity (“doing”), emotional abilities (“feeling”), and rapport (“relating”). The findings provide a systematic categorization of imaginations of GenAI for EMS, showing that GenAI is not only used as an informational tool but also imagined sometimes as an all-knowing, powerful, and highly interpersonal being. These imaginations can be highly relevant for examining human–AI relationships and underscore the need to examine how such imaginations relate to benefits and risks of AI chatbot use for mental health.

items.title: A bibliometric study of human factors in artificial intelligence mediated second language learning ecosystems
items.abstract: This bibliometric study maps the intersection of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and educational technologies, identifying a research gap in the lack of systematic mapping of AI engagement with human affective and cognitive factors in modern pedagogy. To address this gap, we analyzed 3,048 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus from 2015 to 2025 using the Bibliometrix R-package. We captured three thematic clusters: (1) AI integration with motivational factors, (2) human-centric elements including psychological aspects, and (3) educational technologies with a focus on learner-centered pedagogy. Centrality metrics identified “motivation” as a bridge, while the trend topic analysis revealed a growing shift toward Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). This study proposes a new conceptual framework, the AI-Mediated SLA Ecosystem, which integrates human-centric psychological dimensions as a core pillar and offers a roadmap for designing more human-centered AI learning environments.

items.title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
items.abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: A prospective method to support Unmanned Aircraft Systems operators in the application of Specific Operations Risk Assessment
items.abstract: Within the current European regulatory framework, in order to be authorised to perform Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) flights under the specific category of operations, applicants are required to conduct an operational risk assessment. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) selects the Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) methodology as its recommended means to perform this risk evaluation. However, some aspects of this methodology and its application are left relatively open, especially regarding the compliance with the requirements of its safety measures, called Operational Safety Objectives (OSOs). This might complicate the application of SORA, which would benefit from further guidance for its quantitative implementation. Seeking to streamline some aspects of this methodology, this paper presents the Fish Shoal Method (FSM), which combines SORA with two widespread risk analysis methods: bow-tie and Fault Tree Analysis. The synthesis of these methodologies results in a novel method that aims to provide clarity to SORA and to support applicants in the task of determining if their safety requirements are properly substantiated. The practical feasibility of FSM is demonstrated through a worked numerical example of a real UAS operation, focused on the requirements of the procedure-related OSO#08. FSM serves as a guidance to assess the performance of OSOs and make a preliminary estimation of whether the target level of safety of the operation is achieved. Since FSM formalises the main elements of SORA following a causality approach, it also allows the identification of those safety-critical items of the UAS operation that may require further attention. The outcomes of this practical example show that, even in low-risk operations, where the requirements of safety measures are less stringent, the target level of safety for OSOs aimed at human factors are too demanding from a quantitative point of view.

items.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
items.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

items.title: AI Literacy and Genz’s Intentions to Reduce Digital Habits: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Approach for Mindful Technology Usage, Digital Self-Efficacy, and Peer Influence through PLS-SEM, ANN, and fsQCA
items.abstract: Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. items.title: AI-Driven Decision Support Systems in Education: A PRISMA 2020 Systematic Review of Applications, Adoption Conditions, and Decision-Making Outcomes
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS) are increasingly used to inform the decisions of learners, teachers, and administrators, yet evidence on how these systems are applied, adopted, and evaluated remains fragmented. This systematic review, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, synthesized research on AI-DSS in educational settings. Searches of PubMed and Google Scholar (614 records), supplemented by 92 records identified through other methods, yielded 706 records; after deduplication and a relevance-ranked screening cap, 500 records were screened, 56 full texts were assessed, and 54 studies were included in a narrative synthesis that graded each reported outcome by the type of evidence supporting it. Six application domains were identified, led by adaptive and personalized learning and by academic performance prediction and early warning. Machine learning was the predominant approach (89% of studies), whereas explainable AI was incorporated in fewer than one quarter of studies. Adoption depended on institutional support, technical infrastructure, data quality, user-centered design, and stakeholder trust; recurrent barriers included data privacy, model opacity, algorithmic bias, implementation cost, and resistance to change. Reported benefits included more efficient assessment, earlier identification of at-risk learners, and better-informed decisions; however, comparative evidence came mainly from health-professions education, and several headline effects derived from predictive scenarios, technical reports, or single-site evaluations. Subgroup-disaggregated evidence on algorithmic equity was scarce. The review proposes an integrated decision-centered framework linking technological features, institutional conditions, human factors, and calibrated trust to appropriate use, decision quality, and educational outcomes. Advancing the field will require explainable, ethically governed, human-centered systems evaluated through longitudinal, comparative, and equity-sensitive research.

items.title: AI-Driven Real-Time Ergonomic Risk Assessment Framework for Manufacturing Workers
items.abstract: Despite the widespread use of ergonomic assessment tools such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), these are typically applied on an ad-hoc basis by trained assessors and capture only a small, non-random sample of a worker's actual postural exposure. This study proposes, implements and validates a real-time, AI-based ergonomic risk assessment system that combines camera-based human pose estimation with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) data to continuously compute REBA-equivalent risk scores and to provide real-time postural-correction alerts to workers on the shop floor of a medium-scale manufacturing company in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The framework was deployed with 42 assembly-line workers in a mid-sized discrete-manufacturing facility over a 10-week period (4 weeks baseline, 6 weeks intervention), and the AI-generated risk scores were compared against masked manual REBA scores obtained by two certified ergonomists. The AI system achieved 89.6% overall agreement with the manual assessment (weighted kappa = 0.85) and a strong correlation with manual scores (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). The mean weekly REBA score fell from 6.95 to 4.80, and the number of high-risk posture events fell from about 18.5 to 6.5 events per worker-shift, while self-reported musculoskeletal discomfort on the Standardised Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire decreased across all six body regions measured, particularly the lower back (51.3% to 35.7%) and shoulders (44.2% to 31.5%). The results suggest that sensor-fused AI-based ergonomic monitoring can significantly enhance the scalability and objectivity of postural risk surveillance relative to periodic manual assessment, and that when combined with real-time worker-facing feedback, it can measurably lower biomechanical risk exposure and self-reported discomfort within a single production quarter.

items.title: Analyzing Eye-Tracking Indicators of Situation Awareness to Support Human-AI Teaming Under Varying Workload Conditions
items.abstract: Ensuring high levels of Situation awareness (SA) is essential for air traffic controllers (ATCOs), enabling them to continuously process and integrate information into a comprehensive understanding of the situation as it dynamically changes. In the context of human-automation collaboration, SA becomes even more critical, as operators must be prepared to take over control in emergency situations. Although existing studies have largely assessed SA as either poor or good, limited research has explored identification of SA levels (Level 1, 2, and 3). To investigate the potential of eye-tracking technology for real-time SA levels assessment, we conducted an SA-inducing experiment involving 18 participants. Participants are required to perform a series of air traffic control (ATC) tasks corresponding to three SA levels, while their eye-tracking data were simultaneously collected. Eye-tracking features are analyzed using a two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Results identified total fixation duration, number of fixations, average pupil diameter and average amplitude of saccades as key indicators for distinguishing SA levels. Additionally, our findings highlight a significant interaction between SA levels and workload, demonstrating that the effectiveness of these metrics varies under different workload conditions. These insights contribute to enhancing real-time SA evaluation in the safety-critical environments like ATC, further improving the overall operational efficiency and safety in various human-automation collaboration scenarios.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Middle and Secondary Education: Instructional Opportunities, Limitations and Ethical Considerations
items.abstract: Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

items.title: Automation, AI and the Changing Skills Demand for University Graduates: A Comparative Qualitative Study across Four Economic Sectors
items.abstract: Automation, digitalization, and, more recently, generative artificial intelligence (gAI) are changing the skill sets employers demand. However, understanding remains limited about how different sector-level stakeholders in developing countries perceive these innovations, and about these technologies' impact on university graduates' employability. The comparative qualitative study draws on 60 interviews with graduates, employer representatives and academics, five of each type per sector, in four Bangladeshi sectors (readymade garments and textiles (RMG); information and communication technology and IT-enabled services (ICT/ITES); banking and financial services; logistics and supply chain management), as well as multi-sector comparative data. Reflexive thematic analysis yielded cross-sector themes, which include framing of technology and specific discussion of AI in ICT/ITES, disciplinary expertise being necessary but no longer sufficient, with digital, data and adaptive capabilities increasingly essential and learned largely outside formal programmes, cross-sector problems with institutional coordination due to curricula lag (the mode and extent of lag varies according to discipline), reasons why these results should not be taken as an indication of job loss and the impact of gAI, as well as sector-specific and generic implications for universities, sectors and employer associations with clear links to the data. Shortcomings include reliance on perceptions, small cell sizes across multiple parameters, and a lack of a worker perspective.

items.title: Benefits and Barriers to Human-AI Teaming for Crisis Counseling
items.abstract: Background: AI systems are increasingly deployed to support mental health clinicians, yet real-world evidence remains limited. In crisis counseling, where clients often seek human connection, understanding whether AI augmentation preserves or undermines meaningful human engagement is essential. Methods: In a mixed-methods study of a counselor-facing AI copilot on a WhatsApp-based crisis hotline in India (Mar.-Oct. 2025), counselors could request, edit, and send AI messages. We analyzed 20 interviews, 8 shadowing sessions, 56 survey responses, and edits in 27,778 copilot messages from 108 counselors via thematic analysis (Technology Acceptance Model 2, plus inductive coding of emergent factors), and survey statistics. Results: Counselors reported high copilot acceptance (survey): 98.2% found it helpful; 89.3% likely to continue use; 80.4% reported efficiency gains. Interviews highlighted sentence scaffolding, empathetic phrasing, stress reduction, catching missed details, and efficiency. Barriers (survey) included repetitive outputs (23.2%), lack of context (17.9%), and authenticity concerns (10.7%). While 69.6% (survey) reported skill enhancement, interviews surfaced skill atrophy concerns. Counselors frequently accepted copilot suggestions, editing to remove questions, adjust tone, or personalize style. Conclusion: In one of the largest real-world deployments of a counselor-facing mental health AI copilot, counselors reported reduced cognitive load, empathetic communication, and greater efficiency, alongside concerns about skill atrophy, authenticity, and over-reliance. In settings like crisis counseling where clients seek human connection, AI tools must balance operational support with preserving clinical skill and genuine therapeutic engagement. Designs soliciting approval or editing of complete drafts may overweight efficiency at the expense of sustained human engagement.

items.title: Better Questions or Better Questioning? Student-AI Co-Creation and Higher-Order Thinking in Transdisciplinary Engineering and Design Education
items.abstract: As higher education increasingly adopts transdisciplinary frameworks to address complex societal challenges, cultivating students’ higher-order thinking (HOT) skills has become a key educational goal. These cognitive processes are essential in Human Factors Engineering (HFE), which requires students to address wicked problems inherent in transdisciplinary human-technology systems. However, traditional HFE curricula often emphasise rote memorisation of scientific theories. Meanwhile, the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has altered how students engage with academic content by enabling instant access to AI-generated responses. Despite increasing interest in AI-assisted learning, empirical evidence examining LLMs as co-creative partners in activities designed to support HOT remains limited. This quasi-experimental study compares two cohorts in an undergraduate HFE course, in which students either generated exam questions independently or co-created questions with an LLM. A total of 166 multiple-choice questions were collected and classified according to Bloom’s Taxonomy by two independent raters. Results indicate that the LLM-collaboration group produced a significantly higher proportion of higher-order questions. Among student-level factors, the number of student-AI dialogue turns was associated with question cognitive level, whereas self-reported AI usage frequency, metacognitive awareness and prior AI experience were not. Additionally, whether students adopted the AI’s suggested question or wrote their own after the dialogue did not affect question cognitive level. An exploratory analysis suggested that the number of turns in which students critically engaged with AI outputs was marginally associated with higher question cognitive level. These findings highlight the potential value of student-AI dialogue logs as a complementary source of assessment evidence.

items.title: Bridging the Learning Gap in 3D Modelling: Design of an Interactive Topology Feedback System for Blender
items.abstract: Complex 3D environments like Blender present a steep learning curve for novices, where topological errors often remain hidden until the final stages of a project. From a Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) perspective, supporting these users means moving away from static tutorials and toward active, real-time guidance. To explore this, we introduce “Learn & Fix,” a functional prototype Blender add-on with a rule-based architecture that detects mesh flaws in real time and helps new users by explaining their mistakes. We conducted a formative usability pilot study (N = 8) with absolute beginner users (less than 20 h of use) to evaluate interface discoverability, perceived usefulness, and interaction friction. Questionnaire responses highlighted an onboarding discoverability issue, as testers struggled to start the add-on in Blender’s native UI. User feedback indicates that in-viewport validation helps learners spot structural errors early. The design of an educational add-on must balance native UI integration with clear visibility.

items.abstract: OFFICIAL DESCRIPTION OF THE SCIENTIFIC WORK | INTERNATIONAL CATALOG 2026 RESEARCH TITLE: BUILD OR DESTROY: A CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF THE TRANSFORMATIVE POTENTIAL AND DISINFORMATION RISKS OF MODERN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE LEAD RESEARCHER: Dr. Dieudelin Arcangel Legrand - Brotherswagg Robert Academic Jurisdiction and Country of Origin: Republic of Haiti PRIMARY PUBLISHING HOUSE: BrotherswaggStudioRecords Publishing (BSR Publishing) / TM3 MUSIC GROUP INSTITUTIONAL CORPORATE AUTHORSHIP, APPROVAL AND EDITORIAL REVIEW ENDORSEMENT: International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC) and its International Research Consortium: - The Hellenic Institute (Critical Thinking and Theoretical Frameworks) - The Atlantic Research Group (Factual Analysis and Global Perspective) - The Euro-Academic Council (Literary Standards and European Editorial Review) - The Oxbridge Academic (Methodological Rigor and Technical Review) - The Continental Bureau (Source Documentation and Multilingual Research) INTERNATIONAL EDITION: November 2026 ORIGINAL LANGUAGE OF PUBLICATION: Spanish (Official Master Edition) --- 1. SCIENTIFIC CLASSIFICATION AND EPISTEMOLOGICAL NATURE OF THE WORK This publication belongs to the genre of the Critical Review Scientific Article, Epistemological Analysis, and Technological Foresight (an In-Depth Argumentative Scientific Essay). By virtue of its interdisciplinary structure, the work is classified within the fields of Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, and Philosophy of Technology, while establishing direct analytical connections with Communication Studies, Digital Sociology, Applied Ethics, Cognitive Psychology of Perception, and Cyber Law. Having undergone a rigorous process of methodological auditing and structural verification under the standards of the International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC), this research distinguishes itself from conventional technical literature through its comprehensive scope and unwavering commitment to empirical truth. It is neither a merely descriptive manual nor a speculative pamphlet, but rather a reference work designed to diagnose, with surgical precision, the most consequential technological phenomenon of our time. 2. WHY THIS WORK IS ESSENTIAL READING IN THE 21ST CENTURY Humanity is experiencing a historic moment in which the boundary between the real and the artificial has been erased by the speed of algorithms. Every day, millions of people interact with texts, voices, photographs, and video sequences that appear to reflect authentic events but have actually been entirely fabricated by generative artificial intelligence systems. Faced with this unprecedented reality, global society oscillates between two equally dangerous extremes: naïve fascination with the power of machines and uninformed panic in the face of a technology that few people fully understand. "Build or Destroy: A Critical Analysis of the Transformative Potential and Disinformation Risks of Modern Artificial Intelligence" was conceived to dispel this conceptual fog. This work confronts readers with an unavoidable question: How is it possible that the same technology capable of saving lives in medicine, accelerating scientific discoveries, and democratizing education has simultaneously become the preferred tool of countless digital content creators for falsifying reality, impersonating identities, and monetizing deception on a planetary scale? Through rigorous, direct, transparent prose, free from corporate constraints, the Lead Researcher, Dr. Dieudelin Arcangel Legrand - Brotherswagg Robert, together with the IIAEC collegiate body and BSR Publishing, exposes the hidden mechanisms behind this duality without barriers or concealment. Readers who explore these pages will encounter documented truths about how the attention economy operates, why digital platforms amplify synthetic falsehoods, and how society can defend its right to truth without renouncing scientific progress. 3. THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE WORK: AN EVOLUTIONARY NARRATIVE IN FOUR FOUNDATIONAL MODULES To provide a progressive, logical, and deeply enriching reading experience, this research has been structured into seven sections organized around four foundational modules that evolve as one continuous scientific narrative: - FIRST FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | Recent Evolution and Future Horizons of AI: Guides readers from the origins of symbolic computing to the transformer revolution, multimodal foundation models, and emerging autonomous agentic systems, clearly explaining how machines acquired the ability to synthesize realities indistinguishable from the physical world. - SECOND FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | The Constructive and Transformative Potential: Rigorously documents the positive side of this revolution, demonstrating how artificial intelligence is transforming medical diagnosis, drug design, climate sustainability, space research, the inclusion of persons with disabilities, and the democratization of knowledge in every corner of the planet. - THIRD FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | The Anatomy of Deception and a Critical Examination of Malicious Use: Constitutes the critical and revealing core of the manuscript. It examines with intellectual courage how numerous unscrupulous content creators exploit AI to manufacture deepfakes, clone human voices, fabricate pseudo-scientific or pseudo-journalistic evidence, and operate artificial engagement farms, thereby undermining the historical principle of audiovisual evidence and profiting from public credulity. - FOURTH FOUNDATIONAL MODULE | Ethical Discussion, Governance, and the Future of Trust: Proposes concrete solutions to the epistemic crisis by establishing the principles of mandatory transparency, cryptographic traceability from the point of origin, the legal shared responsibility of digital platforms, and the urgent need for critical literacy among citizens. 4. RELEVANCE TO UNIVERSITIES, RESEARCHERS, STUDENTS, AND SOCIETY This work has been conceived as an indispensable reference resource for multiple sectors of the global community: - For Researchers and Academics: It offers an interdisciplinary theoretical framework integrating algorithmic engineering, epistemology, and digital sociology, supported by cutting-edge technical references and international standards. - For Universities and Academic Institutions: It constitutes a bibliographic resource of significant educational value for courses in technological ethics, social communication, computer science, digital law, and contemporary philosophy. - For Students and Young Creators: It provides a moral and technical compass for understanding the power of the tools at their disposal, inspiring them to use artificial intelligence to build genuine knowledge and reject the culture of digital fraud. - For Citizens, Journalists, and the General Public: It delivers the practical and conceptual tools necessary to protect independent judgment against media manipulation and distinguish genuine progress from synthetic illusion. 5. A UNIVERSAL INVITATION: A WORK FOR EVERYONE, BREAKING DOWN BARRIERS AND BUILDING KNOWLEDGE WITHOUT BORDERS Beyond its methodological rigor and technical soundness, this research carries a fundamental declaration of principles: genuine scientific knowledge does not belong to closed elites or intellectual monopolies; it belongs to all humanity. For far too long, the production and validation of global knowledge have been concentrated within hermetic academic canons that erected invisible barriers—geographical, economic, linguistic, and racial—to determine who had the right to conduct research, publish, and be heard. Conceived in the Republic of Haiti with a global outlook and supported by the alliance between BrotherswaggStudioRecords Publishing (BSR Publishing) / TM3 MUSIC GROUP and the International Institutional Academic Editorial Committee (IIAEC), this work deliberately breaks through these historical barriers. It demonstrates that cutting-edge critical thinking, scientific excellence, and the ethical defense of truth can and must emerge from the Global South and reach the entire world, engaging in dialogue on equal terms with institutions across every nation. For this reason, an open, fraternal, and universal invitation is extended to all readers, students, professors, universities, independent researchers, artists, journalists, and citizens of every nation, origin, and circumstance: this work belongs to you. Every page of this study contains essential truths for understanding the world in which we live and defending the future we share. The entire global community is invited to read this article with a critical mindset, debate its arguments in classrooms and across digital networks, cite its findings, translate its message, and actively contribute to the development of an open, inclusive body of scientific literature, free from intellectual racism and committed to human dignity. Because only when knowledge is freed from chains and shared without exclusion does science fulfill its noblest purpose: to illuminate the minds of all human beings. items.title: Designing Cognitive Scaffolds for Generative-AI-Assisted Introductory Programming
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make introductory programming tasks easier to complete, but a working program is not evidence of durable learning. This conceptual-theoretical paper integrates research on cognitive load, metacognition, self-explanation, productive failure, appropriate reliance on automation, and recent studies of AI-assisted programming to propose a five-phase cognitive-scaffolding framework. Learners first make an unaided attempt, request bounded assistance, verify the response against requirements and independently designed tests, explain the mechanism and calibrate confidence, and then complete a related transfer task as support fades. AI literacy, ethical disclosure, privacy, and instructor orchestration operate across all phases. The framework identifies process evidence that remains inspectable when generated code is available, including problem representations, hypotheses, verification records, explanations, confidence judgments, and unaided transfer. It also states six testable propositions and an evaluation blueprint for introductory programming courses. The contribution is a bounded design logic, not a claim that the sequence has already been validated: GenAI should reduce avoidable burden while leaving consequential decisions, checks, and explanations with the learner.

items.title: Designing metacognitive scaffolding in flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning: Evidence from geometry instruction
items.abstract: The development of students’ visual–spatial reasoning is a persistent challenge in geometry learning, where abstract representations and spatial transformations require high levels of cognitive engagement. Although flipped learning has been widely implemented to promote active learning, its effectiveness largely depends on the quality of instructional design and pedagogical support provided during in-class activities. This study investigates how metacognitive scaffolding can be intentionally designed and embedded within flipped learning to enhance students’ visual–spatial reasoning. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed in secondary geometry instruction involving 62 students assigned to experimental and control groups. Quantitative data were collected through pre- and post-tests of visual–spatial reasoning, while qualitative data were obtained from classroom observations and semi-structured teacher interviews. The results indicate that students who experienced metacognitive scaffolding within a flipped learning environment demonstrated significantly greater gains in visual–spatial reasoning than those in a conventional flipped classroom, with a large effect size. Qualitative findings further reveal that scaffolding prompts supported students’ planning, monitoring, and reflective evaluation during problem-solving activities. Overall, the findings suggest that flipped learning environments become more cognitively productive when structured metacognitive scaffolding is deliberately incorporated into the learning design.

items.title: Digital enablement and employee performance in society 5.0: a dual-path model of motivation and exhaustion
items.abstract: Introduction Society 5.0 integrates advanced digital technologies with human-centered work systems, yet its implications for sustainable employee performance remain underexplored. Drawing on Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examines the relationship between Society 5.0 enablement intensity (S5EI) and sustainable human performance through autonomous motivation and emotional exhaustion, considering human-centric governance capability as a moderator. Methods The study employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyse data collected from 519 employees working in digitally intensive sectors in India. Results The findings indicate that S5EI is positively associated with sustainable human performance, primarily through autonomous motivation. Emotional exhaustion partially offsets this positive effect through competitive mediation. Human-centric governance capability strengthens the relationship between autonomous motivation and sustainable human performance but does not significantly buffer the negative effect of emotional exhaustion. Discussion The findings conceptualize digital enablement as a dual-valence work condition that simultaneously strengthens autonomy-based motivation and increases digital demands, integrating Job Demands–Resources Theory and Self-Determination Theory. The study highlights the importance of participatory digital governance, workload management, and employee recovery measures for supporting sustainable human performance.

items.title: Digital Transformation Through a Socio‐Technical Systems Lens: Women Leaders' Approaches to Technological Change and Organizational Dynamics
items.abstract: Organizations navigating digital transformation face persistent challenges integrating social and technical elements to support innovation and worker wellbeing. Despite increasing workforce participation, women remain underrepresented in senior leadership roles that shape how this integration occurs, leaving perspectives shaped by gendered organizational experience underexplored within digital transformation research. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with sixteen senior women leaders across Australian organizations, this study applies socio‐technical systems theory and a gender‐informed leadership perspective to examine how these leaders understood and navigated the relationship between technical and social domains during digital transformation. Participants treated technical and social considerations as mutually constitutive, enacting their integration through communication, employee participation, human‐centered work design, capability development and ongoing adaptation. Psychosocial safety emerged across technical, social and integration‐focused accounts as a system‐level condition implicated in this process. Together, these findings provide an empirical account of human‐centric transformation within Industry 5.0 and extend socio‐technical systems theory by conceptualizing integration as an enacted process through which technical and social considerations continually shape one another. A gender‐informed analysis further demonstrates the value of gendered organizational experience for understanding how socio‐technical integration is accomplished in practice.

items.title: Does Generative AI Reduce Mental Effort at The Expense of Deep Thinking? An Experimental Investigation of Cognitive Load and Knowledge Retention
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has transformed learning practices, raising critical concerns regarding its influence on cognitive engagement, analytical reasoning, and knowledge retention. This study experimentally examines whether GenAI-assisted learning reduces cognitive load at the expense of deep thinking and sustained knowledge acquisition. A randomized controlled experimental design was employed involving 120 undergraduate students, randomly assigned to an experimental group utilizing ChatGPT (n = 60) and a control group completing equivalent learning activities without AI assistance (n = 60). Participants undertook analytical reading, conceptual problem-solving, and critical reasoning tasks under standardized experimental conditions. Cognitive load was measured using a mental effort rating scale, deep thinking was assessed through rubric-based analytical reasoning evaluations, and knowledge retention was examined using immediate and delayed post-tests administered two weeks apart. Results revealed significantly lower perceived cognitive load among AI-assisted learners (M = 3.42, SD = 1.11) compared with the control group (M = 5.76, SD = 1.24), t(118) = 10.88, p < .001. Conversely, students learning without AI demonstrated superior deep-thinking performance (M = 78.40, SD = 9.65) relative to AI-assisted participants (M = 70.25, SD = 10.82), p < .001. Immediate knowledge retention scores showed comparatively modest differences between the experimental and control groups (82.30% versus 80.10%, respectively). However, delayed retention assessments revealed a substantial performance advantage for the control group (74.60%) over AI-assisted learners (65.20%), indicating greater knowledge deterioration following AI-supported learning. These findings suggest that although GenAI effectively reduces perceived mental effort during academic tasks, such efficiency gains may coincide with diminished analytical engagement and weaker long-term knowledge retention. The study extends cognitive load theory and cognitive offloading perspectives by identifying a potential trade-off between immediate learning efficiency and sustained cognitive development. The findings underscore the importance of pedagogically structured GenAI integration that encourages independent reasoning, active knowledge construction, and meaningful cognitive engagement rather than passive dependence on AI-generated responses. Implications for instructional design, assessment practices, and responsible AI adoption in higher education are discussed.

items.title: Effect of Facilitated Problem-Based Learning on Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation Among Nursing Students in North-East Nigeria
items.abstract: This study investigated the effect of facilitated Problem-Based Learning (PBL) on intrinsic and extrinsic motivation among nursing students in North-East Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pre-test, post-test control group design was adopted. The population comprised 1,065 ND II nursing students from six Colleges of Nursing Science in North-East Nigeria, from which 200 students were selected using a multi-stage sampling procedure. The sample consisted of 100 students in the experimental group exposed to facilitated PBL and 100 students in the control group taught using conventional lecture-based instruction. Data were collected using a 28-item Academic Motivation Questionnaire (AMQ). The instrument demonstrated satisfactory reliability with a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.84. The experimental group participated in a six-week facilitated PBL intervention involving nursing-related case scenarios, guided questioning, collaborative learning, feedback, and self-directed learning activities. Data were analyzed using means, standard deviations, and t-tests at the 0.05 level of significance. Finding showed that the experimental group recorded an increase in mean intrinsic-motivation scores from 26.30 at pre-test to 50.30 at post-test, compared with an increase from 25.90 to 30.20 in the control group. A significant effect was also found on extrinsic motivation, with the experimental group recording a greater reduction in extrinsic motivation than the control group, t(198) = 8.72, p < .05. therefore, motivation also differed significantly between the facilitated PBL and lecture groups, t(198) = 14.02, p < .001. Furthermore, a significant difference was observed between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, t(198) = 6.85, p < .001. The study concluded that facilitated PBL is an effective instructional approach for strengthening intrinsic motivation and promoting more self-directed learning among nursing students. It was recommended that nursing institutions should integrate facilitated PBL into their programmes, train educators in effective PBL facilitation, provide adequate learning resources, and emphasize learning activities that foster students’ intrinsic motivation.

items.title: El Rol Humano en la Automatización Inteligente de Procesos Administrativos con IA generativa: Revisión Crítica de la Literatura
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents are entering administrative processes. This marks a shift from robotic process automation to intelligent automation and raises the question of what role people keep when systems process, analyze, and make decisions. The objective was to critically analyze the literature from 2020 to 2026 on the competencies that are transformed or emerging, and on research trends and gaps. A critical and integrative documentary study was carried out in Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, Redalyc, Dialnet, and Google Scholar. It included peer-reviewed studies in Spanish and English, which were analyzed with an extraction matrix and a thematic synthesis. Based on the reviewed literature, GenAI cuts writing time by up to 40% and raises productivity by 15%, especially among novices. However, greater trust in it reduces critical thinking. The emerging competencies are data analysis, digital and complex cognitive skills, decision-making, and continuous learning. Qualitative and short-term studies predominate. There are gaps in the quality of oversight, in Latin American contexts, SMEs, and the public sector, and in the development of expertise. The human role is shifting from execution to oversight and governance. It is effective only under adequate conditions and complying with a protocol is not enough.
