items.title: Relación de la ergonomía con la calidad de vida del docente universitario
items.abstract: Introduction: University professors, immersed in demanding and highly technologized work environments, face conditions that compromise their physical, cognitive, emotional, and social well-being. In this context, ergonomics emerges as a key discipline to mitigate disergonomic risks and foster healthy work environments. Objective: Characterize the relationship between ergonomic factors (physical, cognitive, organizational, and environmental) and the quality of life of university professors, based on the most recent scientific evidence. Methods: An integrative review of scientific literature published between 2019 and 2024 was conducted in the databases Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and Redalyc. Search strategies combined Boolean operators (“ergonom*” AND “university professor” AND “quality of life”) with equivalent MeSH and DeCS terms. Eligible documents included peer-reviewed articles, empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria considered thematic relevance, methodological rigor, and full-text availability. A total of 52 studies met the inclusion criteria. Results: Ergonomic factors are closely associated with the overall well-being of university faculty. Ergonomic interventions improve musculoskeletal health, reduce cognitive fatigue, promote job satisfaction, and optimize the environmental conditions of academic work. Conclusions: Ergonomics, when addressed holistically and at the institutional level, represents a key strategy for enhancing the quality of life of university professors. Its systematic implementation fosters professional performance and helps prevent occupational diseases.

items.title: Revisiting warranting theory in AI-mediated communication: An evaluation of writer and source effects in online reviews.
items.abstract: This article examines how attributing the actual writer of an online message to artificial intelligence (AI) , rather than a human, shapes impression formation . By drawing on and extending warranting theory, this article examines how source role labels (self vs. third party) and content writer labels (AI vs. human) interact to affect impression formation and message effects in the context of hotel reviews. Two preregistered experiments (Study 1: N = 461; Study 2: N = 444) found that, for the same positive hotel review, third-party reviewers were perceived more favorably than self-reviewers (i.e., hotel managers), leading to more positive evaluations of the hotel. Reviews attributed to AI writers negatively impacted impressions of the reviewer and diminished the review’s impact, with third-party reviewers more negatively affected by AI writer labels than self-reviewers. AI labels of user-generated content, therefore, attenuate the effects of source role and move people out of their default impression formation state. We demonstrate theoretical advancements for warranting theory and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: Scaffolded large language model feedback builds durable translation competence whereas unrestricted use fosters dependency
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.

items.title: Short-term cognitive impairments during night work: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Cognitive performance is used as a proxy for work performance and safety. This meta -analysis and systematic review compared cognitive performance during night shifts (23:00–07:00) with daytime performance (07:00–23:00) across experimental field and laboratory studies, excluding shifts exceeding 24 h. Meta-regressions examined night shift, study context, and cognitive test characteristics as sources of heterogeneity. Fifty-five studies were included, yielding 758 night work and 964 daytime datapoints from 1,919 participants, combined into 6135 effect sizes. Cognitive performance was impaired during night shifts relative to daytime hours (Hedges g = −0.36, 95% CI [−0.49, −0.23], p < 0.001), although indications of publication bias suggest this pooled estimate is somewhat inflated. Impairments increased with time into the shift, from 0:01–08:59 h (g = −0.33, 95% CI [−0.63, −0.02], p = 0.041) to > 9 h (g = −0.61, 95% CI [−0.96, −0.25], p = 0.004). Impairments were more pronounced on simple tests (g = −0.50, 95% CI [−0.70, −0.31], p < 0.001), as complex tests weakened the night-daytime difference (g = 0.29, 95% CI [0.07, 0.50], p < 0.001). This contrast was driven by the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT); excluding PVT data removed the difference and attenuated the pooled effect to g = −0.24. No significant moderating effects emerged for time point during the shift, shift sequence, test outcome, or study context (field vs. laboratory). Extended night shifts thus appear detrimental to safety, with heightened sensitivity concentrated in psychomotor vigilance type tasks. Both contexts appear valid for examining these effects. Remaining heterogeneity warrants further investigation of environmental and individual factors.
